newsitem.title: UK: More Europeans could join US fighter plane project.
newsitem.headline: More Europeans could join US fighter plane project.

text.p: French and German aircraft firms could join Lockheed Martin in its bid to win the $100 billion-plus U.S. Joint Strike Fighter project, a senior company executive said on Thursday.

Dain Hancock, president of Lockheed Martin Tactical Aircraft Systems, told Reuters that St Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, Dassault Aviation and Daimler-Benz AG unit Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa) have all been talking with Lockheed about getting work.

It was unlikely that any of the three would have a role in building the two 'concept demonstrator' aircraft needed for the bid, but they could play a part in subsequent development and production work, he said.
"At this point it is dialogue to see where they can be competitive," he told Reuters after a company news briefing in London.
"The question now is what can they (Aerospatiale, Dassault and Dasa) bring to the eventual full-scale development and production programme."

Last month British Aerospace joined the Lockheed and Northrop Grumman team to develop and build the two concept demonstrator aircraft needed for their bid against Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas for what promises to be the Pentagon's biggest ever single aircraft order.
BAe was invited to join the bid to add its expertise in Harrier vertical and short take-off and landing (VSTOL) technology as well as its lean production techniques.

The British firm was also assured of a place on one of the JSF teams because Britain's Ministry of Defence has contributed 200 million pounds ($327 million) to the Pentagon's $1.4 billion initial development programme to find a replacement for its own navy's Sea Harriers.

The JSF is being developed to be a single-type aircraft with variants to eventually replace some 3,000 U.S. Air Force and Navy F-16 and F-18s as well as U.S. Marine Corp and British Royal Navy Harrier 'jump jets'.
With a target price tag of $30 million per aircraft before in-service costs, the winning bid would be worth well in excess of $100 billion for the U.S. orders alone.
But JSF is also being developed for export sales, which industry executives say could eventually win orders for another 2,000 to 3,000 aircraft.
